title: Navigation in Cruising Flight — Use of Fixes to Revise Navigation Data

intro.en: Rev 1 — narration from the recording, cleaned ("crews" → cruise, "a beam" → abeam, "offc course / offcourse" → off-course, "1 in60 / one in 60" → 1-in-60, "onederee / 1°ree" → one degree, "elapse time" → elapsed time, "0.25 25 hours" → 0.25 hours, "recomputee" → recompute, "offtrack / realworld" → off-track / real-world). Before teaching: (1) page 7 (NDB abeam) slide formula "Distance = (GS × Time × Angle) ÷ 60 = 270 NM" is WRONG. Correct: distance run = GS × t ÷ 60 = 120 × 3 ÷ 60 = 6 NM; distance abeam = distance run × tan(first relative angle off the nose) = 6 × tan 45° = 6 NM (the recording is right). Confirm whether the fleet still has ADF and which NDBs remain in service in Thailand before teaching it as a practical method (SME); (2) pages 8–9 and the recording: the "intercept heading change = off-track ÷ distance remaining × 60" gives only the CLOSING ANGLE. To regain track at the next waypoint the heading change is TRACK ERROR + CLOSING ANGLE: 5 NM off after 150 NM gone, 100 NM to go → TE = 2°, CA = 3°, alter heading 5° towards the track; on regaining track turn back by the CA only (3°), keeping the 2° drift correction. The slide/recording "turn 3° toward the track" would not reach the track by the waypoint; (3) page 12 (wind) slide: "wind component = √(GS² − TAS²)" and the wind-direction formula with the answer 112° are wrong (the recording itself says the shortcut is wrong). With TAS 120 kt, TH 100°, TMG 095°, GS 130 kt the actual W/V is ≈ 230°/15 kt (components: tailwind ≈ 9.5 kt, crosswind ≈ 11.3 kt from the left). Solve it on the CRP/E6B wind side; (4) page 4: in controlled airspace, inform ATS if the average TAS at cruise differs by ±5 % or more from the flight plan (ICAO Annex 2 3.6.2.2) and do not change an assigned speed without approval; for the fleet, any speed increase stays below Vno and below Va in turbulence (C172S POH — confirm values; T206H / DA42 HS-NAS POH — SME); (5) page 6: the recording repeats page 5 word for word — narrate the three key points instead (written below).
intro.th: Rev 1 บทบรรยายจากคลิป แก้คำผิดจากคำบรรยายอัตโนมัติแล้ว ก่อนสอน: (1) หน้า 7 (ระยะ abeam NDB) สูตรบนสไลด์ "Distance = (GS × Time × Angle) ÷ 60 = 270 NM" ผิด ที่ถูกคือ ระยะที่บิน = GS × t ÷ 60 = 120 × 3 ÷ 60 = 6 NM ระยะ abeam = ระยะที่บิน × tan(มุม relative แรกจากหัว) = 6 × tan 45° = 6 NM (คลิปถูก) ยืนยันว่าฝูงบินยังมี ADF และ NDB ใดในไทยยังใช้งานก่อนสอนเป็นวิธีปฏิบัติจริง (SME) (2) หน้า 8–9 และคลิป: "heading change = ระยะออก track ÷ ระยะที่เหลือ × 60" ให้แค่ CLOSING ANGLE ถ้าจะกลับเข้า track ที่ waypoint ถัดไป ต้องเปลี่ยน heading = TRACK ERROR + CLOSING ANGLE ออก track 5 NM หลังบิน 150 NM เหลือ 100 NM → TE = 2°, CA = 3° เปลี่ยน heading 5° เข้าหา track เมื่อกลับเข้า track แล้วหันกลับเท่า CA (3°) และคงการแก้ drift 2° ไว้ การ "เลี้ยว 3° เข้าหา track" ตามสไลด์/คลิปจะไม่ถึง track ที่ waypoint (3) หน้า 12 (ลม) สไลด์: "wind component = √(GS² − TAS²)" และสูตรทิศลมที่ได้คำตอบ 112° ผิด (คลิปเองก็บอกว่าทางลัดนี้ผิด) ด้วย TAS 120 kt, TH 100°, TMG 095°, GS 130 kt ลมจริง W/V ≈ 230°/15 kt (ลมส่ง ≈ 9.5 kt, crosswind ≈ 11.3 kt จากซ้าย) ให้แก้บนด้าน wind side ของ CRP/E6B (4) หน้า 4: ในห้วงอากาศควบคุม ให้แจ้ง ATS ถ้า TAS เฉลี่ยขณะ cruise ต่างจากแผนการบิน ±5 % ขึ้นไป (ICAO Annex 2 3.6.2.2) และห้ามเปลี่ยนความเร็วที่ ATC กำหนดโดยไม่ได้รับอนุญาต สำหรับฝูงบิน การเพิ่มความเร็วต้องต่ำกว่า Vno และต่ำกว่า Va ในอากาศแปรปรวน (POH C172S ยืนยันค่า; T206H / DA42 HS-NAS POH — SME) (5) หน้า 6: คลิปพูดซ้ำหน้า 5 ทุกคำ ให้บรรยายสามประเด็นสำคัญแทน (เขียนไว้ด้านล่าง)

pages.on: Title and two intro paragraphs; airliner photo.
pages.en: In cruising flight, good navigation is less about holding a line and more about continuously proving that your plan still matches reality. Your planned course, estimated ground speed and forecast wind give you a calculated position, but the atmosphere is never perfectly stable: winds change with altitude, temperature and time, and small errors can build up quietly over long legs. This section focuses on the practical techniques pilots use to stay accurate and safe in the cruise: taking regular fixes, comparing them with the dead-reckoning position, and then revising the numbers that drive the rest of the flight. When you update your ground speed from observed fixes, you can immediately refine your ETA and make better decisions about fuel, alternates and workload. When you recognise that you are drifting off track, you can apply simple, fast correction methods to regain the planned route without over-controlling or guessing. And when you understand how drift reveals the wind effect, you can adjust headings and anticipate whether your progress will improve or worsen on the next segment. These techniques are equally valuable for students building confidence and for experienced pilots managing longer flights. The goal is to stay ahead of the aircraft: confirm your position, update the plan, and communicate early if a significant speed or route change is needed. That disciplined cycle — fix, compare, revise — turns cruise navigation into a controlled, predictable process rather than a hopeful estimate.

pages.t: Ground-Speed Revision: On-the-Fly Flight Planning Adjustment
pages.on: Infographic: 1 find remaining distance, 2 calculate time remaining, 3 calculate required GS; example 50 NM in 0.5 h → 100 kt.
pages.en: To revise ground speed in the cruise, you are answering one practical question: what ground speed do I need from here to meet the planned arrival time at the next waypoint? This simple technique helps you stay on schedule and immediately shows whether you need a heading change, a power adjustment or a revised estimate. Start by finding the remaining distance to the target waypoint. Use your chart, GPS or navigation display to confirm how many nautical miles are left. Make sure you use the distance along your intended track to the waypoint, not an unrelated distance to a nearby feature. Next, calculate the time remaining: take the time you want to arrive at the waypoint and subtract the present time. Convert minutes to a fraction of an hour so the calculation stays consistent — 30 minutes becomes 0.5 hours, 15 minutes 0.25 hours and 45 minutes 0.75 hours. Accuracy matters here, because a small timing mistake can produce a large speed error. Then calculate the required ground speed by dividing the remaining distance by the time remaining. This gives a target number you can compare with your current ground speed. If the required ground speed is close to what you are making, your plan is still realistic. If it is significantly higher or lower, decide what adjustment is appropriate: changing power, choosing a different cruise altitude for a better wind, or revising the ETA and telling whoever needs the update. In the example, with 50 nautical miles remaining and 0.5 hours to reach the waypoint, the required ground speed is 50 divided by 0.5, which is 100 knots. This quick revision keeps cruise navigation realistic, supports fuel planning and helps you manage timing accurately across several waypoints.
pages.th: การปรับ ground speed ขณะ cruise คือการตอบคำถามเชิงปฏิบัติข้อเดียว ต้องใช้ ground speed เท่าไรจากตรงนี้เพื่อให้ถึง waypoint ถัดไปตามเวลาที่วางแผน เทคนิคง่าย ๆ นี้ช่วยให้ตรงเวลา และบอกทันทีว่าต้องเปลี่ยน heading ปรับกำลังเครื่อง หรือแก้ค่าประมาณเวลา เริ่มจากหาระยะทางที่เหลือถึง waypoint เป้าหมาย ใช้แผนที่ GPS หรือจอนำทางยืนยันว่าเหลือกี่ไมล์ทะเล ต้องเป็นระยะตาม track ที่ตั้งใจถึง waypoint ไม่ใช่ระยะไปยังจุดอื่นใกล้ ๆ ต่อไปคำนวณเวลาที่เหลือ นำเวลาที่ต้องการถึง waypoint ลบด้วยเวลาปัจจุบัน แปลงนาทีเป็นเศษส่วนของชั่วโมงเพื่อให้คำนวณสอดคล้อง 30 นาทีเป็น 0.5 ชั่วโมง 15 นาทีเป็น 0.25 ชั่วโมง และ 45 นาทีเป็น 0.75 ชั่วโมง ความแม่นยำสำคัญตรงนี้ เพราะเวลาผิดนิดเดียวทำให้ความเร็วผิดมาก แล้วคำนวณ ground speed ที่ต้องการโดยนำระยะทางที่เหลือหารด้วยเวลาที่เหลือ ได้ตัวเลขเป้าหมายที่เทียบกับ ground speed ปัจจุบันได้ ถ้าใกล้เคียงกับที่ทำได้อยู่ แผนยังสมจริง ถ้าสูงหรือต่ำกว่ามาก ต้องตัดสินใจว่าจะปรับอย่างไร เปลี่ยนกำลังเครื่อง เลือกความสูง cruise อื่นที่ลมดีกว่า หรือแก้ ETA และแจ้งผู้ที่ต้องรู้ ในตัวอย่าง เหลือ 50 ไมล์ทะเลและมีเวลา 0.5 ชั่วโมงถึง waypoint ground speed ที่ต้องการคือ 50 หาร 0.5 เท่ากับ 100 นอต การปรับแบบเร็วนี้ทำให้การเดินอากาศขณะ cruise สมจริง สนับสนุนการวางแผนเชื้อเพลิง และช่วยจัดการเวลาได้แม่นยำในหลาย waypoint

pages.on: Three blocks: Wind Impact (increase airspeed for headwinds…), Airspeed Limits, ATC Communication (obtain clearance before a significant speed change); cockpit photo.
pages.en: These considerations keep a ground-speed revision realistic and safe, especially in the cruise, where small changes can have operational and regulatory consequences. Wind impact: ground speed is your true progress over the ground, and it is strongly influenced by wind — a headwind reduces it and a tailwind increases it. If your required ground speed is not being met, the first step is to recognise whether the wind is the cause, and by how much. You can respond by adjusting power and airspeed when appropriate, but also by considering a change of altitude if it offers a better wind component. The important point is that you are managing the resulting ground speed, not chasing airspeed numbers without understanding the wind effect. Airspeed limits: a required ground speed is only useful if it is achievable within the aircraft and operational limits. Any increase in airspeed must stay within the aircraft's performance, its operating limitations and any applicable restrictions, such as turbulence penetration speed, manoeuvring speed and airspace speed limits. Also consider the fuel: a higher airspeed normally increases fuel flow, which may affect endurance and reserve planning. If meeting the original timing would mean pushing beyond reasonable limits, it is safer to revise the arrival time than to force the aircraft to make the maths work. ATC communication: if achieving the required ground speed means a significant speed change, coordinate with air traffic control. Speed changes can affect separation, sequencing and spacing in controlled airspace. Inform ATC early, state your requested speed or your inability to maintain an assigned speed, and comply with any clearance or instruction. Clear communication prevents conflicts, reduces workload for everyone and keeps your flight predictable and safe.
pages.th: ข้อพิจารณาเหล่านี้ทำให้การปรับ ground speed สมจริงและปลอดภัย โดยเฉพาะขณะ cruise ที่การเปลี่ยนแปลงเล็กน้อยอาจมีผลด้านการปฏิบัติการและข้อกำหนด ผลของลม ground speed คือความก้าวหน้าจริงเหนือพื้น และได้รับผลจากลมมาก ลมปะทะลด ground speed ลมส่งเพิ่ม ground speed ถ้าทำ ground speed ที่ต้องการไม่ได้ ขั้นแรกคือดูว่าลมเป็นสาเหตุหรือไม่และมากแค่ไหน ตอบสนองได้ด้วยการปรับกำลังและความเร็วอากาศเมื่อเหมาะสม และพิจารณาเปลี่ยนความสูงถ้าได้องค์ประกอบลมที่ดีกว่า ประเด็นสำคัญคือเราจัดการ ground speed ที่ได้ ไม่ใช่ไล่ตามตัวเลขความเร็วอากาศโดยไม่เข้าใจผลของลม ขีดจำกัดความเร็ว ground speed ที่ต้องการมีประโยชน์ก็ต่อเมื่อทำได้ภายในขีดจำกัดของเครื่องและการปฏิบัติการ การเพิ่มความเร็วต้องอยู่ในสมรรถนะของเครื่อง ขีดจำกัดการใช้งาน และข้อจำกัดที่เกี่ยวข้อง เช่นความเร็วสำหรับบินผ่านอากาศแปรปรวน maneuvering speed และขีดจำกัดความเร็วของห้วงอากาศ และต้องคิดถึงเชื้อเพลิง ความเร็วสูงขึ้นปกติทำให้ fuel flow เพิ่ม ซึ่งอาจกระทบ endurance และแผนเชื้อเพลิงสำรอง ถ้าการทำให้ทันเวลาเดิมต้องดันเกินขีดจำกัดที่สมเหตุสมผล การแก้เวลาถึงปลอดภัยกว่าการบังคับเครื่องให้ตัวเลขลงตัว การติดต่อ ATC ถ้าการทำ ground speed ที่ต้องการหมายถึงการเปลี่ยนความเร็วมาก ให้ประสานกับ ATC การเปลี่ยนความเร็วมีผลต่อการแยกระยะ ลำดับ และระยะห่างในห้วงอากาศควบคุม แจ้ง ATC แต่เนิ่น ๆ บอกความเร็วที่ขอหรือแจ้งว่ารักษาความเร็วที่กำหนดไม่ได้ และปฏิบัติตาม clearance หรือคำสั่ง การสื่อสารที่ชัดเจนป้องกันความขัดแย้ง ลดภาระงานของทุกคน และทำให้เที่ยวบินคาดการณ์ได้และปลอดภัย

pages.on: Infographic: 1 measure distance between two fixes, 2 calculate elapsed time, 3 compute average GS; example 60 NM in 0.5 h → 120 kt.
pages.en: Average ground speed in the cruise is calculated from what actually happened between two confirmed fixes. It is one of the most reliable ways to update your navigation numbers, because it is based on measured distance and measured time, not forecast assumptions. Measure the distance: identify two known fixes on your route — charted waypoints, a radio fix or clearly confirmed visual checkpoints — and determine the distance between them from your navigation display, the chart scale or the planned leg distance. Use nautical miles so the result comes out in knots. Calculate the elapsed time: record the time at the first fix and at the second fix, then find the difference. Convert minutes to a fraction of an hour so the calculation is consistent — 30 minutes is 0.5 hours, 15 minutes is 0.25 hours and 45 minutes is 0.75 hours. Compute the average ground speed: divide the distance by the elapsed time. This gives the average ground speed you actually made good over the ground between the two fixes. You can then use that value to revise the ETA, the fuel plan and the timing of the remaining legs. In the example, if you fly 60 nautical miles in 0.5 hours, the average ground speed is 60 divided by 0.5, which is 120 knots.

pages.t: Average Ground Speed Calculation: Key Points
pages.on: Three boxes: Units (NM and kt), Accuracy (fix and time precision), Wind Impact (GS is not TAS).
pages.en: [The recording repeats the page 5 narration word for word here; use this written narration.] Three key points make your average ground speed trustworthy. First, units: keep distance in nautical miles and time in hours, or use the computer with minutes against the 60 index, so the answer comes out in knots. Mixing kilometres, statute miles or minutes without converting is the most common classroom error. Second, accuracy: the result is only as good as the two fixes and the two times. Use fixes you are certain of, read the time when you are actually overhead, and use a long enough distance so that small timing errors do not distort the answer. Third, wind impact: the average ground speed is what the aircraft made good over the ground, including the wind; it is not your true airspeed. The difference between the two is the head- or tailwind component you are really experiencing, and that is exactly the information you use to revise the ETA, the fuel and, with the track made good, the actual wind.

pages.t: Distance to NDB Abeam Position Calculation
pages.on: Infographic: time from relative bearing 045°/315° to 090°/270° (3 min); slide formula "Distance = (GS × Time × Angle) ÷ 60"; example "= 270 NM".
pages.en: To estimate your distance from an NDB when you are abeam it, you use the change in relative bearing and the time between those two bearings. First, start the timing when the relative bearing to the NDB is 45° — the station is ahead and to one side. Stop the timing when the relative bearing reaches 90°, the abeam position. Next, convert the elapsed time into distance travelled over the ground: multiply your ground speed by the time in minutes, then divide by 60. With a ground speed of 120 knots and a time of 3 minutes, the distance travelled is 120 × 3 ÷ 60, which is 6 nautical miles. Then convert that distance travelled into the distance to the station abeam, using the tangent of the initial angle. Because the initial angle is 45°, the tangent is one, so the distance abeam is the same as the distance travelled. In this example the aircraft is 6 nautical miles from the NDB when it is abeam.

pages.on: Infographic: 1 measure off-course distance (5 NM), 2 note total distance flown (150 NM), 3 apply 1-in-60 → track error 2°.
pages.en: The 1-in-60 rule is a fast mental method for estimating how many degrees you are off track and how much correction you need to get back on course. First, measure how far off course you are — the lateral distance from your planned track to your actual position. You might get this from a fix plotted on the chart, a GPS cross-track error or a confirmed visual reference. Next, note the total distance flown since your last known position on track, in nautical miles. Then apply the 1-in-60 rule: track error angle in degrees equals the off-course distance divided by the distance flown, multiplied by 60. In the example, you are 5 nautical miles off course after flying 150 nautical miles: 5 divided by 150 is 0.033, and multiplied by 60 gives about 2°. That means your track is about 2° away from where it should be. To correct back onto track, pilots apply two parts. First, correct by the track error to stop the drift; and second, add a closing angle to regain the track within a reasonable distance. This keeps the correction simple, controlled and easy to monitor.

pages.t: Heading Change to Intercept Track: Off-Course Correction Guide
pages.on: Infographic: 1 measure off-course (5 NM), 2 note remaining distance (100 NM), 3 "Heading Change Angle = off-course ÷ remaining × 60 = 3°", 4 apply correction.
pages.en: When you find you are off track, the quickest way to touch the track is to turn 90° towards it. That works in the sense that it reduces the cross-track error rapidly, but it is usually not efficient: a 90° turn stops your progress towards the waypoint, increases the distance flown, and can create a second correction later when you have to turn back onto course. A better technique is to choose an intercept angle that brings you back to the planned track while you continue moving generally towards the waypoint. This keeps progress steady, reduces wasted distance and is easier to manage in the cruise. To do this, measure how far off course you are and note the remaining distance to the next waypoint. Use the 1-in-60 relationship to find the closing angle: closing angle in degrees equals the off-course distance divided by the remaining distance, multiplied by 60. For example, if you are 5 nautical miles off track with 100 nautical miles remaining, that gives about 3°. [Corrected:] Add this closing angle to the track error you found on the previous page — 2° — so you alter heading 5° towards the track, and monitor that the cross-track error is reducing. If you are right of track, steer left; if you are left of track, steer right. As you rejoin the track at or before the waypoint, turn back by the closing angle only, so you keep the 2° correction for the wind, and avoid overshooting. This method is both practical and efficient: it corrects the error while still flying forwards, keeping your timing, fuel planning and workload more stable than a sharp 90° correction.

pages.en: The 1-in-60 rule is a simple mental relationship between angle, distance flown and sideways error. It is used because small navigation angles behave almost linearly, which makes quick estimates possible in the cockpit. The core idea: if you fly 60 nautical miles with a 1° track error, you end up about 1 nautical mile off track. The same relationship scales up and down: at 120 nautical miles a 1° error gives about 2 nautical miles off track; at 30 nautical miles a 2° error gives about 1 nautical mile. That is why it is called 1 in 60 — 1° produces 1 nautical mile of lateral displacement after 60 nautical miles. From the same idea you can rearrange the formula to solve what you need. Track error angle in degrees equals off-track distance divided by distance flown, times 60. Closing angle in degrees equals off-track distance divided by distance remaining, times 60. Off-track distance in nautical miles equals the angle in degrees divided by 60, times the distance. These are cockpit-friendly because you can estimate them quickly without a calculator. How pilots use it in flight: confirm how far you have drifted — after a fix, estimate the track error angle and see whether the problem is small and stable or growing. Choose an efficient intercept — instead of turning 90° towards the track, pick a modest angle that brings you back while still making progress towards the waypoint. And build confidence in your wind correction — if your track consistently differs from the plan, 1 in 60 helps you estimate how many degrees of heading change will hold the desired track. The strength of the rule is not perfect precision; it is speed, simplicity and accuracy good enough for safe, timely decisions. Put another way: if after flying 60 nautical miles you are 1 nautical mile to one side of your intended track, your track error is about 1°; if you are 2 nautical miles off after 60, the error is about 2°, and so on. To use it operationally: one, get a fix and measure how many nautical miles you are left or right of the planned track; two, measure the distance gone since you last knew you were on track; three, compute the track error angle; four, decide the correction. A heading change equal to the track error will usually stop you getting further from the track; to get back onto it within a reasonable distance, add a closing angle on top, based on how quickly you want to rejoin. Remember the limitation: it is an approximation, most accurate for small angles and moderate distances. For higher precision use the navigation computer, electronic systems or trigonometry, but for fast in-flight decisions the 1-in-60 rule is often the most practical first answer. The key phrase to remember: after 60 nautical miles, 1° equals 1 nautical mile.

pages.en: Drift angle is the angular difference between where the aircraft is pointing and where it is actually moving over the ground — in practice, the wind's sideways effect on your track. Formula and sign: a common way to compute it is drift angle equals track made good minus true heading. If the result is negative, the track is left of the heading, meaning left drift; if it is positive, the track is right of the heading, meaning right drift. Example: track made good 095°, true heading 100°; drift angle = 095 − 100 = −5°. That means the aircraft is drifting 5° to the left: the ground track is left of where the nose is pointing. To interpret it operationally, remember that drift has a size — how many degrees — and a direction — left or right. If you want to maintain a desired track, apply a wind correction angle into the wind; in simple terms, adjust the heading so that the resulting track made good lines up with the required track. Using an average drift angle over a leg is useful, because the wind varies and a single momentary value may not represent the overall effect. What influences drift? It changes with wind speed and with wind direction relative to your heading, and it can also vary with aircraft speed and altitude, because the wind often changes through the atmosphere. If precision is required, use reliable fixes and tools to confirm the track made good rather than relying on a single estimate.

pages.en: To calculate wind speed and direction in flight, it helps to think of one simple picture: the aircraft has one motion through the air, and the wind moves that air mass over the ground. What you observe over the ground is the combination of the two — that is why we use the triangle of velocities. Start with what each value really means. True airspeed is how fast you are moving through the air mass. True heading is the direction the nose is pointing, referenced to true north. Ground speed is how fast you are moving over the ground, and track made good is the direction you actually move over the ground. The difference between true heading and track made good is the drift, which tells you whether the wind is pushing you left or right. The first step is usually to confirm the ground speed from fixes: pick two reliable fixes, measure the distance between them in nautical miles, and record the time taken in hours. Distance divided by time gives ground speed in knots — a real, observed number that automatically includes the wind's effect. A common mistake is to try to get the wind speed with a shortcut such as the square root of ground speed squared minus true airspeed squared. That only works in a very special case, when the wind is exactly perpendicular to the air vector. In real flying the wind is rarely at exactly 90°, so the shortcut can give wrong or even impossible answers. The correct approach uses the full triangle: the wind speed depends on the true airspeed, the ground speed and the angle between the air vector and the ground vector, which is the drift. If you know how fast you move through the air, how fast you move over the ground and how far the track is displaced from the heading, you can solve for the wind, whatever its direction. To find the wind direction, the most reliable method is to work in components: break the motion into north and east parts, once for the air vector, using TAS and true heading, and once for the ground vector, using ground speed and track made good. The wind vector is simply the ground vector minus the air vector; its length gives the wind speed and its angle gives the direction. Finally, remember the reporting convention: wind direction is given as the direction the wind comes FROM, so you add 180° to the direction the vector points towards. One more important point: drift alone is not enough. With only TAS and drift you cannot determine the wind; you also need the ground speed and either the track made good or the true heading to complete the triangle. That is why accurate fixes and accurate timing matter: the better your inputs, the more useful the calculated wind, especially as winds vary with altitude and time. In practice pilots use this wind to refine dead reckoning, improve the ETA and confirm whether a heading correction is still appropriate. It is not about producing a perfect number, but about getting a reliable wind picture that supports safer, more accurate navigation. [Worked example, corrected: TAS 120 kt, TH 100°, GS 130 kt, TMG 095° → W/V ≈ 230°/15 kt.]

pages.on: Three steps: time to destination = remaining distance ÷ revised GS; ETA = current time + time to destination; update flight plan (inform ATC if significant); example 80 NM at 120 kt → 40 min, 13:00 → 13:40 UTC; moving-map photo.
pages.en: ETA revisions using observed fixes are a practical cruise habit, because they keep your flight plan realistic. Winds often differ from the forecast, and small timing errors can compound over a long leg. By routinely updating your ETA you stay ahead of the aircraft, manage fuel and workload better, and are ready to answer accurately when air traffic control asks for an estimate at a waypoint or destination. Start by getting an observed, revised ground speed: use your last two reliable fixes and calculate the average ground speed from the measured distance and elapsed time. This revised ground speed is more trustworthy than the original plan because it reflects what the aircraft is actually achieving over the ground. Next, calculate the time to destination: take the remaining distance to the next waypoint or destination and divide it by the revised ground speed. This gives time in hours, which you convert to minutes for a quick operational picture. For example, with 80 nautical miles remaining and a revised ground speed of 120 knots, 80 divided by 120 is two-thirds of an hour — 40 minutes. Then determine the new ETA by adding the calculated time to the current time: if it is now 1300 UTC, adding 40 minutes gives an ETA of 1340 UTC. Finally, update your flight plan and cockpit notes. Record the revised estimate for the waypoint and the destination, and update any downstream timing such as top-of-descent planning or fuel checks. If the change is significant, be prepared to inform air traffic control, especially in controlled airspace, where sequencing, traffic flow and coordination depend on accurate estimates. This simple cycle — fix, revise ground speed, recompute time, update the ETA — keeps your navigation accurate and your communications confident.

pages.on: Three numbered items: one-in-sixty rule, continuous updates, wind and drift calculations; "Remember": wind, aircraft performance, ATC.
pages.en: Mastering in-flight navigation is mainly about staying ahead of the aircraft by making small, timely corrections based on what you observe in the air, not just what you planned on the ground. The 1-in-60 rule: use it as your quick mental tool to estimate the track error and choose an efficient intercept. It helps you correct back towards the track without wasting distance on large turns, and gives you a practical way to decide how many degrees of heading change are needed. Continuous updates: treat ground speed and ETA as living numbers. After each reliable fix, update the average ground speed from distance and elapsed time, then revise the time to the next waypoint and the destination. This keeps your plan accurate, supports fuel management and lets you answer confidently when air traffic control asks for an estimate. Wind and drift calculations: wind is often the hidden cause of timing errors and off-track drift. Use drift and track made good to recognise the wind effect early, adjust the heading with an appropriate wind correction angle, and do not let small deviations grow. Better wind awareness also supports more accurate fuel and endurance planning. Keep these real-world factors in mind: the wind can change with altitude and time; aircraft performance limits the speed you can realistically achieve; and ATC instructions such as speed control or holding can shift your estimate. So revise early and communicate clearly when the change becomes significant.
